newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Archbishop voted Zaire parliament speaker.
newsitem.headline: Archbishop voted Zaire parliament speaker.

text.p: Zaire lawmakers on Saturday voted Archbishop Laurent Pasinya Monsengwo as speaker of the transition parliament, assembly spokesmen said.
The vote makes him a potential interim successor to President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"Monsengwo has just been voted by near unanimity as speaker of parliament," Christophe Lutundula, second deputy speaker of parliament from the moderate opposition, told Reuters.

"He is not an alternative to either President Mobutu or Kabila," Kutundula said, referring to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces have seized about three-quarters of Zaire and are closing in on the capital in a drive to topple Mobutu.
"We are hoping he will play a role as a national mediator and will persuade all sides to agree on a way of safeguarding the democratic process in Zaire," Lutundula added.

The vote, conducted by a show of hands, was marred by a prior walkout by the UDPS radical opposition party of Etienne Tshisekedi, and it was not clear whether a quorum was achieved nor whether the "consensus" vote would prove binding.

Diplomats said the popular archbishop is in Rome. The parliament expected him to return to Zaire early next week after being notified of the results of Saturday's vote but it was not clear whether he would accept the post.
Foreign diplomats involved in trying to broker a peaceful resolution to the seven-month-old conflict in Zaire see the post of speaker as a key element in any peaceful settlement.

A regional crisis summit of francophone African states held in Gabon and attended by Mobutu this week asked Zaire's parliament to proceed with the election of a president "to allow normal functioning of institutions and favour an orderly and democratic transition."
According to Zaire's transition constitution, the speaker of parliament succeeds the president in the event of his death or incapacity.
The post has been vacant since a combined move by Mobutu followers and MPs of the radical opposition ousted Monsengwo two years ago.
At the time Mobutu's followers accused the popular archbishop of being too close to the opposition, while Tshisekedi's followers said he was weak in the face of Zaire's president of three decades.
The UDPS on Friday reiterated objections to Monsengwo's candidacy, calling him a "Mobutist."
However, Monsengwo according to many Zaireans is one of the few leading figures with the popular credibility and reputation for neutrality necessary to arbitrate among the country's politicians.
His appointment would allow Mobutu the possibility of standing down without leaving a power vacuum in his wake.

Some diplomats and political leaders say it would provide the ailing president -- who is battling cancer as well as the rebellion -- the dignified exit necessary to forge an agreement between Zaire's warring factions.
Rebels say any peace agreement should involve Mobutu's resignation and a direct handover of power to Kabila.
